title: IMSA Closed Out 2026 with Petit Le Mans, and It Was a Humdinger

body_markdown:
What an odd, and consistently interesting, the season finale for the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship turned out to be. Although there was only one genuinely scary crash, the race was a bit of a mechanical bloodbath: This[Motul Petit Le Mans,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/expect-a-damp-full-house-at-imsas-petit-le-mans-finale/) held as it has been since 1998 at Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta, set a record with 17 yellow-flag caution periods, plus a 30-minute, full-stop red flag to clear the track of standing water following a rainstorm.


If you’re a fan of sports car racing, it’s likely you already know that one of the two[Porsche Penske 963 GTP](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/at-85-roger-penske-just-cant-stop/) cars won the battle, taking the overall victory. But Cadillac won the war, scoring enough points early on to wrap up the manufacturers’ championship, and the drivers’ championship for the number 31 Action Express, Whelen-sponsored racer Jack Aitken.


At 2.54 miles, Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta may sound like a reasonably lengthy track, but the 12-turn circuit seems much shorter. Add to that the huge 54-car field—there was a waiting list of teams that wanted to race, but couldn’t, because 54 is the absolute number of pit boxes available—and the leaders began to encounter the tail end of the field just six minutes into the 10-hour endurance race.


At Petit Le Mans, as in all IMSA endurance races, the field was a mix of four classes.


Lumen via Getty Images


With four classes, each averaging different speeds, it’s a toss-up as to who had the toughest job: The fastest class, GTP, having to negotiate around the slowest class, GT Daytona, or the GTD drivers who had to monitor their rearview mirrors constantly as they tried to stay out of the way of the typically faster GTP, Le Mans Prototype 2, and GTD Pro cars.[Here’s a link](https://imsa.results.alkamelcloud.com/Results/26_2026/21_Road%20Atlanta/01_IMSA%20WeatherTech%20SportsCar%20Championship/202610031210_Race/10_Hour%2010/03_Results_Race_Provisional.PDF) to the provisional race results.


The winning LMP2 car, the number 04 Crowdstrike Racing Oreca (all the LMP2 cars are Orecas, powered by a built-in-England Gibson V-8) was six laps behind the top six GTP cars, outrunning four other LMP2 cars that finished on the same lap. The winning GTD Pro car was the number 68 Car Blanche Aston Martin Vantage GT3 Evo, a second and a half ahead of the number 77 AO Racing Porsche 911 GT3 R. In the GTD class, the number 57 Winward Racing Mercedes-AMG claimed the win, finishing 29th overall.


Although Porsche claimed victory in Georgia, Cadillac won the 2026 manufacturers’ title, and Jack Aitken, in the Whelen-entered #31 Cadillac V-Series.R, took the drivers’ crown.


Lumen via Getty Images


GTD and GTD Pro cars are the same, based on actual sold-to-the-public models, with the difference being that GTD is a pro-am class and GTD Pro is, well, strictly professional. The former requires two amateur drivers, either Bronze- or Silver-rated in their licensing, and one pro who is Platinum- or Gold-rated. Teams competing in the latter strictly employ Platinum- or Gold-rated drivers. In the prototypes, LMP2 utilizes a similar driver protocol as GTD.[On this list,](https://www.imsa.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/32/2026/09/23/2026_IWSC_RoadAtlanta_PreEvent_EntryList.pdf) you’ll see the names of each driver with his or her rating in parenthesis as P, G, S or B. Typically the amateurs, often referred to as “gentleman drivers,” pay the team for that privilege, essentially becoming a sponsor. In some cases, the amateur actually owns the team.


With 162 names on the entry list, it is difficult for the driver of an approaching GTP car to know what to expect as it attempts to pass a GTD or LMP2 car. Practically speaking, this means that some cars in GTD and LMP2 may be driven quite well, then after a driver change five minutes later, a bit less well.


I’m not sure how it played out on television, but in person, if it sounds as though this running of Petit Le Mans had a little bit of everything, it certainly did. As mentioned, the[only truly frightening crash](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Flrq4a_lrmQ) was when Kevin Magnussen’s Team WRT BMW GTP car collided with the Meyer Shank Racing Acura GTP, driven by five-time IndyCar champion Alex Palou, which sent Magnussen’s car briefly airborne and hard into the turn 3 tire barrier. Magnussen was able to climb from the done-for-the-day BMW and was released after visiting the care center.


This was the final race for the Acura ARX-06 GTP, as the manufacturer will not return to the series in 2027.


Lumen via Getty Images


This crash occurred minutes after a peculiar incident, when Renger van der Zande, driving the number 93 Meyer Shank Racing Acura GTP car, collided with Meyer Shank teammate Colin Braun in the number 60 Acura. This was the last race for the Acura ARX-06 GTP, as Acura is calling it quits for IMSA racing.
The race began with high hopes for the two Acuras, which qualified first—Tom Blomqvist in the number 60—and second, with Nick Yelloly in the number 93, making for an all-Acura front row. Starting third was the number 24 BMW, qualified by Sheldon van der Linde, and in fourth was Jack Aitken in the number 31 Cadillac.


Only the two Acuras were able to get around the track in less than one minute and 10 seconds, with polesitter Blomqvist notching a 1:09.703 lap. But after that, the field was quite close—the slowest GTP qualifier of the 11 entries was the JDC-Miller Motorsports Porsche 963, with a still-competitive time of 1:11.001. Everyone else in GTP was in the 1:10 range.


In the race itself, Ross Gunn in the number 23 Thor Team Aston Martin Valkyrie GTP set the fastest lap, 1:11.897 on lap 305. That lone Aston Martin GTP car finished fifth, hampered in part by an IMSA-assessed penalty for causing the crash that dropped the number 31 Action Express Cadillac from third place and battling for the lead, to a finish of 16th overall, 12 laps down from the race-winning 368 laps. The winning Porsche 963, driven by the trio of Laurens Vanthoor, Kevin Estre, and Matt Campbell, had a race average of 1:12.179, proving that in endurance racing, you don’t always have to be the fastest to win.


Laurens Vanthoor, Kevin Estre, and Matt Campbell celebrate in victory lane during following their overall victory at the Motul Petit Le Mans in their #6 Porsche Penske Motorsport 963 GTP.


Lumen via Getty Images


There was a distinctive bittersweet-ness to this year’s Petit, as it marked, as mentioned, the last race for the Acura AR-06 in the GTP class. And Lexus, which raced in both the GTD and GTD Pro series, will not return for 2027, after a decade in the series. Both manufacturers are represented by top-notch teams, and while some of the drivers and crew have jobs for next year, others were hoping for a strong Petit to add to their job-wanted resumes.


Though Lexus won’t return, parent company Toyota will, racing its GR GT3 beginning with the Rolex 24, eligible for the GTD and GTD Pro classes. Ford debuts its GTP-level Hypercar in 2027, but it will be racing in the overseas World Endurance Championship, not in IMSA, though it’s expected to compete here in its home market starting in 2028 or ’29. Hyundai will debut its Genesis-branded GTP car in IMSA next year, beginning with the Rolex 24 at Daytona, after spending 2026 racing it in the WEC. Also, 2027 finishes out the final year of the five-year contract between Porsche and Penske, with a genuine wait-and-see beyond that. While mildly updated, Porsche’s current 963 is aging, though last weekend’s Petit Le Mans victory proves that it’s still competitive, after an uneven 2026 season.


One of the toughest jobs IMSA has is determining its “Balance of Performance” standards, where it attempts to create a level playing field among manufacturers by adding or subtracting weight, aerodynamic properties, fuel capacities, and other race-determining factors. For a lengthy period late in the race, the top five consisted of one car from each of the five manufacturers—Cadillac, Porsche, Acura, BMW, and Aston Martin—suggesting that IMSA’s BoP worked pretty well.


Lumen via Getty Images


Lumen via Getty Images


Lumen via Getty Images


Lumen via Getty Images


Indeed, it speaks to the overall health of the[John Doonan-led](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/the-cowboy-who-became-a-sheriff-john-doonan-steers-the-imsa-ship-through-troubled-waters/) IMSA that there was a waiting list of teams wanting to race at Petit, coupled with an enormous crowd for Saturday’s race and a surprisingly big crowd for Friday—which featured the Michelin Pilot Challenge series two-hour race, plus qualifying for Saturday’s main event, and the always-entertaining Mazda MX-5 Cup race, in which very-equal Miatas compete for a full-contact 45 minutes. Won by Parker DeLong, less than one second separated the top five Miatas at the checkered flag.


All of that being a given, it’s the fact that IMSA had 18 manufacturers competing across its seven series this year—from the Ferrari 296 to the Cupra Leon hatchback—which arguably confirms that this may well be the healthiest racing series in the world. NASCAR, which owns IMSA, has three manufacturers in its top-level Cup series, while IndyCar has two. Formula 1 has five engine manufacturers, and its popularity level remains top-rung. But when there are 18 car builders that actually *pay* IMSA for the privilege of racing, it’s not only impressive but essentially unprecedented.


IMSA’s season, beginning in late January and ending with the October Petit, is one of the longest in all of sports. For 2027, it cranks back up with the annual “Roar Before the Rolex” test session at Daytona International Speedway January 22–24, followed by the Rolex 24 at Daytona the next weekend, and ends with Petit Le Mans on October 9.


This year’s Petit Le Mans was a suitable finale to the 11-race season, and I’m already looking forward to the 2027 Roar. The entry list for the Rolex 24 is already full, and as it was at Petit, there are more teams on the waiting list. I wish IMSA had a better, more accessible television package, but beyond that, there just isn’t much here to complain about.
